5.0.0.en: The third sermon begins with a lamentation over the virgin of Israel: 1 Hear ye this word which I take up against you, even a lamentation, O house of Israel. 2 "The virgin of Israel is fallen; she shall no more rise:

5.0.1.en: she is forsaken upon her land; there is none to raise her up." 3 For thus saith the Lord GOD;

5.0.2.en: "The city that went out by a thousand shall leave an hundred, and that which went forth by an hundred shall leave ten, to the house of Israel." [1-3].

5.0.3.en: The word before us is a lamentation which the Lord Himself raised, describing with sorrow the state to which the virgin of Israel had come. Perhaps He called Israel a "virgin" to declare that this lamentation, which is raised over one who has died, was raised over the virgin of Israel, who is like a bride who died in her early youth while still a virgin, before she could enjoy the joy of married life. She is the virgin from whom the Lord expected to have a perpetual bride, but she chose the path of spiritual death, and so lost her life before she could enjoy the life of union with her Bridegroom.

5.0.4.en: Perhaps God called her "the virgin of Israel" as a sign that until this moment she had been the virgin who had not yet been defeated and had not yet fallen under captivity... But by her evil she loses her virginity, indeed she loses all her life. God has a jealousy for her because she is His virgin bride, and the Apostle Paul bore the spirit of his Master when he said: "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ" (2 Cor 11:1-2).

5.0.5.en: The virgin of Israel fell from what she ought to have been, a virgin for the Lord who bears His holiness and His splendor. Sadly she fell and shall no more rise, because she refuses the chastisements of her Bridegroom meant to bring her back to Him; she relied on herself or on others apart from her Bridegroom, and so found no one to raise her up. She was cast down upon her land, a sign of complete weakness, for she did not go out to fight, nor did she withdraw to an outside battlefield, but was defeated before herself, because of her inner weakness. As the Lord Himself says: "A man's foes shall be they of his own household" (Mt 10:36). In our inner Jerusalem we fall when we accept the ego and live for ourselves, not for the Lord who loves us!

5.0.6.en: When a person falls in his inner battle because of the ego, which seeks its own and not what belongs to others, he loses much; if it goes out by a thousand there remain a hundred, and if it goes out by a hundred there remain ten... It loses much, and the small faithful remnant remains preserved with God. This remnant, which represents the tenth in God's eyes, is dear and precious, and He is bound to preserve it for the sake of His faithfulness toward His believers, as we have seen more clearly in more than one place in our study of the book of Ezekiel.

5.0.7.en: God does not forget the hundred for the sake of the remnant of the thousand, nor the ten for the sake of the remnant of the hundred. He did not forget Lot and his two daughters for the sake of the whole region of Sodom and Gomorrah, nor did He forget Noah and his family for the sake of the corruption of the whole world!

5.1.s.en: 2. Seek the Lord, not the idol:

5.1.0.en: 4 For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, "Seek ye me, and ye shall live: 5 But seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought. 6 Seek the LORD, and ye shall live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be none to quench it in Bethel. 7 Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth, 8 Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, and maketh the day dark with night: that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name: 9 That strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress."

5.1.1.en: Having raised a lamentation over the virgin of Israel, He did not stop at the sorrowful description, but revealed the door of deliverance, by turning to God, the Source of life, and abandoning idolatrous worship, saying: "Seek ye me, and ye shall live: but seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba" [4-5].

5.1.2.en: At that time the people bore the outward marks of religiosity, going out to worship at the holy places, but it appears that the worship of God had become mixed with idolatrous worship, especially in the principal centers of Israel: Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba. Or perhaps their worship had become merely a soothing of consciences: they went to those places and offered much to God, but they did not seek Him with their heart, nor keep His commandment in their life and conduct. As I have said before, ritual was separated from the spiritual life among them, and their worship became a means of covering up their wicked attitudes.

5.1.3.en: If we seek the holy places, let our first and last seeking in them be life with God and in Him: "Seek ye me, and ye shall live." Note that the word "seek" does not mean merely asking with the mouth, but the true inner longing for God, the secret of our true life.

5.1.4.en: As St. Augustine says, addressing God, the secret of his life: [How then shall I seek You, O Lord? For when I seek You, my God, I seek the happy life. I seek You that my soul may live, for my body lives by my soul, and my soul lives by You.]

5.1.5.en: Places that were once holy became a stumbling block through idolatrous worship, so He says: "For Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought." Gilgal and Bethel were two holy places, but since man corrupted them, the first place is taken captive and the second is utterly destroyed. When the Samaritan woman said to the Lord Jesus: "Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship" (Jn 4:20), the Master answered her: "Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father... God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" (Jn 4:21, 24).

5.1.6.en: We do not deny that God is pleased even with the holy places which man offers in love to be places of worship for Him, but He rejoices in them for the sake of the person who is sanctified by Him! Even in the consecrated church the heart of the believer rises above all limits of place and time to soar toward eternity, and finds the Spirit of God has lifted him up into heaven itself! I have spoken often before about the church building, its meaning, and its connection with the inner life of the soul as well as with the heavenly and liturgical life. If the house of God loses its spiritual meaning and man is confined to dust and earth, he turns the house of God into an obstacle instead of being the secret of the soul's soaring!

5.2.0.en: The Lord repeats, "Seek the LORD, and ye shall live" [6]. This is the goal of all our worship: to meet our Lord Jesus and seek Him with all the heart as the secret of our life.

5.2.1.en: The Lord threatens: "Lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be none to quench it in Bethel" [6]. Perhaps many of the tribes of Israel used to count the sons of Joseph blessed because the mountain of Bethel had fallen to their lot (Josh 16:1-2), but this mountain became a consuming fire when it was misused. Perhaps it is like the priesthood, which gives a person mighty spiritual and pastoral possibilities, but if it is misused it becomes the very weapon of destruction. And why speak of Bethel or the priesthood, when the Lord Christ Himself, who is the secret of the salvation of many, became by His coming a cause of judgment for those who denied Him, as He says: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloak for their sin... If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father" (Jn 15:22-24). As the Apostle Paul says of the Lord Christ: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: to the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life" (2 Cor 2:15-16).

5.3.0.en: We return to Israel and find that it had mixed the worship of the living God with idolatrous worship, so that Bethel became destruction for the house of Joseph, and here by this is meant all Israel coming to Bethel, for their lives are set ablaze with the fire of evil and there is no one able to quench it. Thus they turn truth into the bitterness of injustice and corrupt heavenly righteousness by casting it to the ground: "Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth" [7].

5.3.1.en: If wormwood is an exceedingly bitter herb thrown on the ground, which man cannot bear, then the truth, which gladdens the heart of God and man, when it is overturned is turned into its opposite and becomes wormwood. So it is with those who have great abilities and gifts: when they are sanctified by the Spirit of truth, mingled with love and humility, they bear witness to the truth and offer, by the Holy Spirit, works to which generations testify and which heaven confirms; but when they go astray they do not stand passive, rather they become bitter wormwood in the mouth of God and His Church, turned into instruments of demolition instead of building. They cast righteousness to the ground, since their thinking burdens them, without their knowing it, with a deadly earthly nature.

5.3.2.en: Therefore let "the LORD" Himself be the object of our constant seeking that we may live, and let us not turn into wormwood or cast righteousness into the dust... But who is this Lord whom we seek?

5.3.3.en: "He that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, and maketh the day dark with night:

5.3.4.en: that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name:

5.4.0.en: That strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress" [8-9].

5.4.1.en: First: the Creator of the Pleiades and the Giant, which are two groups of stars that were famous at that time. If Israel had turned aside to worship the stars, then the true God is the Creator of all the stars, and it is He whom it is fitting for them to seek.

5.4.2.en: The Septuagint rendering of the text brings out that God is the Creator of things and also the One who changes them... St. John Chrysostom has a very bold word, for he sees in God the Creator One who trains us, His children, in the creative life, saying: [God gave us a body from the earth, but so that we might carry it with us to heaven. It is truly an earthly body, but it must be heavenly... It is as though He says: I created heaven and earth, and I gave you the authority to create. Make your earth heaven, for this is within your authority. I am the Creator of things and the One who upholds them [8]. As the Lord Himself says, He gave man a similar authority, as though He were an artist and a tender father teaching his son his art! I created your body beautiful and gave you authority to make something better... For if you cannot create a man, yet you are able (by the Holy Spirit) to make him righteous and acceptable before God. I formed the matter, so you adorn the will! Behold how I love you and entrust to you authority in great matters! Behold what honor is ours!]

5.4.3.en: Second: the God whom we seek turns the shadow of death (the night) into morning, and makes the day dark as night. He is not only the Creator of heaven and earth out of nothing, but He also brings about change: He changes night into morning, and day into night.

5.4.4.en: What is this night, or what He called the shadow of death which was turned into morning, but the fulfillment of the prophecies of the Old Testament and the shadows of the Law, when man had fallen under death as one in the night, into the day of His joyful coming, so that we were enlightened by His divine light? As the prophet says: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined" (Isa 9:2).

5.4.5.en: Let us offer Him our night and He will make it morning; let us hand over to Him all our troubles and sorrows, and He will shine upon us, and they will be turned into spiritual delights, surpassing peace, and glorious joy unspeakable.

5.4.6.en: As for the day which is made dark and becomes night, it reminds us of the divine work during the hours of the crucifixion, when noon turned into darkness because of our sins, which our Redeemer carried on His shoulders. This is the surpassing work of the Lord, who bore our sins in Himself, He who knew no sin!

5.4.7.en: And what is the day that becomes darkness but the day of the wicked, who live in the luxury and pleasures of life, reckoning that the joy of the world does not pass away and that their pleasures never end... But in His love He turns their day into night through His chastisements, which seem harsh, so that they may not be attached to the day of the world and its pleasures!

5.4.8.en: Third: He calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth... that is, He turns the waters of the seas into clouds that cover the earth and rain upon it. We saw in our study of the book of Joel [2:23] that the former rain and the latter rain refer to the grace of the Holy Spirit working in the children of God. So the God whom we seek is the Creator, and He is the One who changes our life by the coming of the Messiah the Savior, and He is the Giver of fruit through the waters of the Holy Spirit, as the Master Himself said: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. (But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given)" (Jn 7:37-39).

5.4.9.en: Though we are earth, the waters of the Holy Spirit turn us into the delightful paradise of God, bearing the fruit of His Spirit in us!

5.4.10.en: Fourth: the God whom we seek, His name is Jehovah (Yahweh). After presenting Himself to us as Creator and Renewer of our nature through the saving work of Christ, and as the Giver of fruit in us by His Holy Spirit, He brought us into His mysteries... He is Yahweh, that is "the One who is," who cannot be comprehended. Though He has drawn very near to us through His saving work and the sending of His Holy Spirit, He remains the God who cannot be approached in the fullness of His essence. We spoke before about the meaning of the name of God "Yahweh" in our study of the book of Exodus (ch. 3).

5.5.0.en: Fifth: the God whom we seek is He "that strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress" [9]. He gives success and strength to the person who has been robbed or plundered against the strong man who wronged him, so that he is able to attack his fortress and recover his stolen right. He is the God who gives victory to the defeated soul and grants it strength and triumph!

5.6.s.en: 3. Injustice in the courts of justice:

5.6.0.en: 10 They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. 11 Forasmuch therefore as your treading is upon the poor, and ye take from him burdens of wheat: ye have built houses of hewn stone, but ye shall not dwell in them; ye have planted pleasant vineyards, but ye shall not drink wine of them. 12 For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right. 13 Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time; for it is an evil time. 14 Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the LORD, the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken. 15 Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the LORD God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph.

5.6.1.en: Among the Jews the courts of justice were held in a public square at the gate of the city (Deut 22:15; Isa 29:21), under the leadership of a judge or prophet who rebuked the wrongdoer and supported the righteous. But sadly the courts of justice were turned into courts of injustice. He says:

5.6.2.en: "They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. Forasmuch therefore as your treading is upon the poor, and ye take from him burdens of wheat: ye have built houses of hewn stone, but ye shall not dwell in them; ye have planted pleasant vineyards, but ye shall not drink wine of them. For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right" [10-12].

5.6.3.en: These are painful manifestations of the injustice that prevailed in the courts of justice. On the one hand, instead of rebuking the wrongdoers, these elders hated the one who rebuked or warned them; they wanted to flatter the wrongdoers at the expense of the truth, so that they hated anyone who spoke a word of truth, because it wounds the rich wrongdoers. On the other hand, instead of lifting the needy from the dunghill, they trampled him underfoot. They demanded of him a gift that was closer to a bribe, and since he had no money to give, they compelled him to give his wheat, and he and his family remained hungry. The Law forbade usury on food (Deut 23:9). Yet these seize the food of the poor so that they may build for themselves houses of hewn stone that cannot give them security, and plant for themselves pleasant vineyards that cannot quench them with the wine of joy.

5.6.4.en: Finally, in their injustice they afflict the just and take the bribe which the Law forbids (Ex 21:30; Num 35:31).

5.7.0.en: And since injustice increased greatly, even in the courts of justice, it was said: "Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time; for it is an evil time" [13]. When a person realizes that his defense of the needy is of no avail, he keeps silent, not out of cowardice or fear of the wrongdoers, but out of wisdom, so as not to waste his time on what is of no avail. St. Basil wrote at the end of his book "On the Holy Spirit," saying: [Since the ordinances of the Gospel have been utterly confused by disorder, the rush to advance to the chief offices has become beyond imagining, and every lover of display puts himself forward before others by force... So the entreaties of the leaders have become barren and vain, because everyone in the seas of his ignorance judges that it is his duty to give orders to others and not to obey anyone himself. For these reasons I have preferred silence to speech, for there is not in a human voice the strength to make itself heard in such a tumult. If the saying of the preacher were true: "The words of the wise are heard in quiet" (Sir 9:7), it would be necessary to refrain from speaking at the present time.]

5.7.1.en: The wise man keeps silent in the evil time and speaks only to the extent that he perceives his words to be of benefit, imitating God Himself, who offers us His divine mysteries only to the extent that we are able to bear hearing them, understanding them or benefiting from them. His mysteries remain hidden until we acquire the spiritual ear able to listen and to grasp the mysteries in a constructive way. From the words of St. Clement of Alexandria: [The Lord says: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear" (Mt 11:15), declaring that hearing and understanding are not for everyone. In this David writes: "He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies. At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire" (Ps 18:11-12), showing that the sacred words are hidden.]

5.8.0.en: The silence of the prudent in the evil time is in itself a witness of truth against injustice and tyranny... But the matter does not end there; rather the Lord demands a return to Him, through the return of these unjust judges or elders from injustice in the court of justice (in the gate), saying: "Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the LORD, the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken" [14]. It is as though He says to them: if you boast that God, the Lord of hosts, is with you and in your midst, then the sign of this is practical conduct: seeking good and rejecting evil; by this you live by the Lord who dwells in your midst.

5.8.1.en: Israel wrongly supposed that God's choice of them as a people exempted them from punishment however much they sinned, and that God dwells in their midst whatever their condition. So God corrects their notions, declaring that His choice of them from among all the families of the earth increases their responsibility and brings them all the more under punishment if they sin (Amos 3:2). And here He affirms that His dwelling in their midst will come only by their seeking the greatest good and rejecting evil in practice in their life and their judgments. Finally, He speaks of His choice of them as making them like grain in a sieve in God's hands: He punishes them severely and deals strictly with them without destroying them (Amos 9:7-10).

5.9.0.en: At the beginning of the sermon He said to them, "Seek the LORD" (Amos 3:6), and here He declares their obligation to seek Him through their practical conduct: "Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the LORD God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph" [15]. Israel will be subjected to bitter chastisements; some of them will die, some will be killed by the sword, and some will be taken captive... But God does not forget the remnant faithful to Him. If it stands firm in the truth, loves the good and hates the evil, He will be gracious to it and declare His dwelling in its midst.

5.10.0.en: 16 Therefore the LORD, the God of hosts, the Lord, saith thus; "Wailing shall be in all streets; and they shall say in all the highways, Alas! alas! and they shall call the husbandman to mourning, and such as are skilful of lamentation to wailing. 17 And in all vineyards shall be wailing: for I will pass through thee, saith the LORD."

5.10.1.en: He concludes the lamentation with God's passing through their midst, not as the secret of their life but to punish and chastise them, so that all Israel turns into a place of mourning and wailing, since all have come into a state of death. God's presence became a cause of sorrow, not of joy!

5.10.2.en: Here he presents a realistic picture of the ancient Eastern mourning, where they hired people who specialized in mournful songs during the funeral rites.

5.11.0.en: This group is in fact part of the third sermon, in which God proclaims woe to the people because of three things:

5.12.s.en: First: desiring the day of the Lord:

5.12.0.en: 18 Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light. 19 As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him. 20 Shall not the day of the LORD be darkness, and not light? even very dark, and no brightness in it? [18-20].

5.12.1.en: God is light, and His day is light in itself, but for the spiritually blind, who cannot behold the light, the light becomes darkness. As St. Basil says: [The day of the Lord is darkness for those who deserve darkness.]

5.12.2.en: The day of the Lord in the mind of the Jews meant God's declaring His power and His victory in His people against their enemies. Therefore it was a day of joy and triumph, a day of boasting over the Gentiles. But since the people were entangled in their many sins and unrepentant transgressions, it was turned into a day of judgment and bitterness.

5.12.3.en: No one can flee from judgment, for the one who flees is like one who flees from a lion and meets a fierce bear, or one who wants to take refuge in his house and puts his hand on a wall to lean on it, and a serpent bites him.

5.13.0.en: This is a clear line in most of the writings of the prophets, for Israel did evil and went to the holy places for public worship, offering burnt offerings and gifts and rejoicing in the feasts... God is not deceived by outward appearances, for He asks first for the heart (Mk 12:33).

5.13.1.en: In bitterness He rebukes them: "21 I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies (your gatherings). 22 Though ye offer me burnt offerings and your meat offerings, I will not accept them: neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat beasts. 23 Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. 24 But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." [21-24]. He rejects outward worship that is not joined to inner love, and He ascribed all the worship to them, not to Himself, saying: "your feast days, your burnt offerings," whereas when God is pleased with them, He reckons them as His feasts, His sabbaths and His burnt offerings, and rejoices to ascribe them to Himself.

5.13.2.en: God cannot bear their praises and hymns, and reckons them as noise: "the noise of thy songs." As the Apostle Paul says: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" (1 Cor 13:1).

5.13.3.en: In order that their worship might be acceptable He says: "Let judgment (justice) run down as waters, and righteousness (almsgiving) as a mighty stream"... that is, let your life be mingled with justice and the love of giving, instead of injustice and cruelty.

5.14.0.en: "25 Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel? 26 But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves. 27 Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus, saith the LORD, whose name is The God of hosts." [25-27].

5.14.1.en: The prophets looked back to the period of the wilderness as the best period Israel lived in its relationship with God (Hos 2:14-16; Jer 2:1-3), as an ideal period in which God provided for Israel in a unique and surpassing way. In this period the Lord did not stress the laws of sacrifices but the moral commandments, and perhaps their wandering in the wilderness made the offering of sacrifices difficult, so we hear that they did not keep the Passover after the second year until their crossing into Canaan.

5.14.2.en: Note here that the prophet Amos did not say: "You did not offer sacrifices and offerings," for he did not deny them altogether, but they were not a goal during their wandering in the wilderness.

5.14.3.en: They mixed the worship of God with idolatry, carrying the tabernacle of "Molech" or "Milcom," the god of the Ammonites, as a god for themselves, heating his arms until they glowed red and then placing children on them amid the beating of drums. They also worshipped gods that are a group of stars and planets. Therefore, as they took themselves captive to idolatrous worship, God humbles them by captivity under the power of idolaters, beyond Damascus (Aram), that is, to the Assyrian captivity, which is far beyond Damascus. They carried idolatry in their heart, so God left them to be carried by the idolaters!
